# Alīnacittajātaka (Ja 156)
**ID:** Ja 156
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Alīnacittajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja156

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Alīnacittajātaka* (Ja 156) is a narrative belonging to the Second Book (*Dukanipāta*) of the Pali Jātaka collection [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1879]. In the framing story set at Jetavana, the Buddha addresses a monk who has slackened his exertion (*ossaṭṭhaviriya*), noting that the complete opening circumstances are related in the Saṁvara Jātaka of the eleventh *nipāta* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The Master admonishes him by recalling how, in a previous birth, he had demonstrated immense determination by securing the kingdom of Benares for an infant heir [SuttaCentral].
In the story of the past, an elephant treated for a severe foot wound by carpenters repays their kindness by assisting them and bequeathing to them his young son [Burlingame 1921; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Following the death of the king of Benares, when the kingdom is attacked by an invading force, the newly born prince, Alīnacitta, and his mother must depend on this noble elephant to confront the enemy, defeat the opposing host, and capture the hostile king [Burlingame 1921; Ohnuma 2012]. The teaching verse illustrates that just as a mighty army was overcome on account of Alīnacitta, so a monk of resolute will attains Nibbāna through earnest effort [Burlingame 1921]. In the *samodhāna*, the Bodhisatta is identified as Prince Alīnacitta, his parents as Suddhodana and Mahāmāyā, the elder grateful elephant as Sāriputta, and the kingdom-winning elephant as the fainthearted monk [Fausböll 1879; Ohnuma 2012].
The episode is also incorporated into the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* to illustrate the Venerable Sāriputta's outstanding gratitude [Burlingame 1921; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal text reuse between Ja 156, the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, particularly across segment ranges §0.4–3.1 [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus reports any cross-language parallels [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§0.4–3.1 ↔ §106–114_0); Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0502a) (§0.4–3.1 ↔ §1562–1567_0)
**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for ja156 — Provides English titles, collection context, and the summary of the opening frame story and dialogue.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus automated text reuse matches for Ja 156 — Reports Pali-internal shared passages with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā and Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā and absence of cross-language matches.
- [Burlingame 1921] Eugene W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends: Translated from the Original Pali Text of the Dhammapada Commentary (1921) — Details the inclusion of the jātaka in the Dhammapada commentary, the story of the carpenters and elephant, verse translation, and book placement.
- [Fausböll 1879] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with Its Commentary, Vol. 2 (1879) — Provides the Pali text incipit, nidāna reference to the Saṁvara Jātaka, and the concluding identification of the characters (samodhāna).
- [Nyanaponika et al. 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha: Their Lives, Their Works, Their Legacy (2003) — Discusses Sāriputta's previous birth as the grateful elephant in relation to the Rādha episode.
- [Ohnuma 2012] Reiko Ohnuma, Ties That Bind: Maternal Imagery and Discourse in Indian Buddhism (2012) — Analyzes the role of the infant prince, the mother (identified as a past birth of Māyā), and the elephant protector in Ja 156.
